summary_student.text: Small gas flames (methane, ethylene, propane and propylene) were burned in a glovebox aboard the International Space Station, with a gentle stream of air around them. The team turned up the fuel until each flame started giving off soot, the dark smoke particles, to see how much fuel a flame can take before it gets smoky. Knowing how soot forms without gravity helps design safer spacecraft.

summary_professional.text: Laminar non-buoyant jet diffusion flames of methane, ethylene, propane, propylene and propylene mixtures were burned in a coflow duct inside the Microgravity Science Glovebox on the ISS, with burner diameters of 0.41 mm, 0.76 mm and 1.6 mm and coflow velocities from 5.4 cm/s to 65 cm/s. Fuel flow rate was adjusted to find the laminar smoke point, the onset of soot emission. Still and video cameras recorded luminous flame length and height, and radiative heat losses and coflow air velocity distributions were measured; in total 526 flames were studied.

pillar.reason: The record states the work will improve understanding of soot formation and help design safer spacecraft environments, and its PSI subarea is Fire Safety; it characterizes when flames start to produce soot rather than detecting or extinguishing fires.
